stem:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to ED by ambulance 90 minutes after ingesting an estimated 60 tablets of her father's amitriptyline 50 mg. She is drowsy but responsive to voice, with a widened pulse pressure and cool peripheries. Her Glasgow Coma Score is 12. Ambulance ECG en route showed a broad QRS complex.

She has a documented depressive disorder and current suicidality was declared to the paramedics. IV access has been established and 500 mL of normal saline has been infused during transport.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, GCS 12, dry mucous membranes, dilated pupils; abdomen soft; no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 132 ms, QT 460 ms, sinus tachycardia; venous gas pH 7.30, HCO3 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L; paracetamol level pending; serum tricyclic assay pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg to reverse suspected co-ingestion of benzodiazepines
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose because it can precipitate seizures, which are dangerous in TCA toxicity due to acidosis lowering seizure threshold. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - TCA)

options.text: Oral activated charcoal 50 g and 4-hourly repeat ECG until QRS returns to normal
options.rationale: Airway is at risk in a drowsy patient; oral charcoal without intubation risks aspiration. IV therapy is required now for the widened QRS. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - TCA)

options.text: Intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg loading dose to shorten the widened QRS
options.rationale: Phenytoin is not first-line for TCA-associated arrhythmia; sodium bicarbonate is the antidote and phenytoin can prolong QT. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - TCA)

options.text: Intravenous 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus for the widened QRS
options.rationale: QRS over 100 ms in TCA overdose is an indication for sodium bicarbonate to correct acidosis, increase sodium load and offset sodium channel blockade; the goal is QRS narrowing and pH 7.45 to 7.55. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - TCA)

options.text: Intravenous intralipid 20 percent 1.5 mL/kg bolus over one minute now empirically
options.rationale: Intralipid is reserved for cardiovascular collapse refractory to bicarbonate; first-line is sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - TCA)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes sodium channel blockade producing QRS widening, hypotension and ventricular arrhythmias, together with anticholinergic and central depressant effects. Indications for sodium bicarbonate include QRS over 100 ms, ventricular arrhythmia, or hypotension not responding to fluids. Dose is 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV boluses with the goal of narrowing QRS and reaching arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55. Airway protection is often required as GCS falls. Intralipid is second-line for refractory cardiovascular collapse. Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdoses because it lowers the seizure threshold.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms in TCA overdose triggers sodium bicarbonate.
Target arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55 with bicarb boluses.
Flumazenil contraindicated; may provoke seizures.
Intralipid is reserved for refractory cardiovascular collapse.
explanation.pearls: In amitriptyline overdose, look at the QRS: over 100 ms means give sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg immediately and repeat until QRS narrows and pH is 7.45 to 7.55.

stem:
A 38-year-old man with schizophrenia has been on olanzapine 20 mg nightly for 12 weeks after an inpatient admission for a psychotic relapse. His weight at commencement was 82 kg and today at community follow-up he weighs 91 kg. He has developed increased thirst and polyuria over the past 3 weeks. He otherwise reports good mood, no psychotic features, and has been adherent.

He smokes half a pack of cigarettes a day, drinks alcohol only socially and has no personal history of diabetes. His father has type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: BMI 29.2; acanthosis nigricans absent; no focal neurological findings
data_table.Investigations: Random glucose 12.8 mmol/L; fasting glucose (deferred but pending); HbA1c 7.2 percent; lipids: total cholesterol 6.4 mmol/L, LDL 4.2 mmol/L, HDL 0.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 3.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step now?

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged and give dietary and exercise advice at review today
options.rationale: New-onset diabetes on olanzapine warrants a change or dose reduction of the offending agent alongside diabetes treatment; lifestyle alone will not offset the drug-induced metabolic effects. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidelines)

options.text: Ask the patient to reduce olanzapine to 10 mg nightly with monthly HbA1c monitoring
options.rationale: Halving the dose maintains high metabolic burden; switching to a lower-risk antipsychotic (aripiprazole) is preferred when new diabetes emerges. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidelines)

options.text: Cease olanzapine tonight without a replacement and offer clozapine within the week
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation risks psychotic relapse; clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant illness and has its own metabolic burden. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidelines)

options.text: Start metformin 500 mg twice daily and continue olanzapine at the current dose
options.rationale: Adding metformin without addressing the causative drug leaves ongoing metabolic drive; guideline-preferred approach is to switch the antipsychotic and manage diabetes alongside. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidelines)

options.text: Cross-taper to aripiprazole, start metformin and refer to diabetes clinic for review
options.rationale: Guideline-preferred approach is to switch from a high metabolic risk antipsychotic (olanzapine, clozapine, quetiapine) to a lower-risk agent (aripiprazole, ziprasidone), start metformin, and coordinate with diabetes services. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics vary substantially in metabolic risk. Olanzapine and clozapine are the highest-risk agents for weight gain, dyslipidaemia and new-onset diabetes; quetiapine is moderate; aripiprazole, ziprasidone and lurasidone are lowest. When metabolic complications emerge, guideline management is to cross-taper to a lower-risk agent while maintaining psychiatric stability, treat the metabolic disorder in parallel (metformin for new diabetes, statin for dyslipidaemia, blood pressure control), and continue metabolic monitoring at least every 3 months. Baseline and 3-monthly weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c, and lipids are recommended.
key_points: Olanzapine and clozapine are highest metabolic risk.
New diabetes warrants switch to lower-risk antipsychotic, not just adjunct.
Aripiprazole, ziprasidone are lowest metabolic risk.
Metabolic monitoring at baseline and 3-monthly.
explanation.pearls: When a patient on olanzapine develops new diabetes, cross-taper to aripiprazole and start metformin; do not just add metformin and continue olanzapine at full dose.

subtopic_detail: Right-sided endocarditis in an IV drug user
stem:
A 32-year-old man with a history of intravenous heroin use presents with 5 days of fevers to 39.5 degrees, rigors, and a dry cough with mild pleuritic chest pain. He last injected 8 days ago. On examination he is warm and diaphoretic with tender needle-track marks in the left antecubital fossa. Chest auscultation is clear. Cardiac auscultation reveals a soft systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge that varies with respiration.

He is hepatitis C positive and untreated, HIV negative on testing 6 months ago. Chest X-ray shows scattered bilateral peripheral rounded infiltrates. Blood cultures have been drawn from two separate sites.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; needle-track marks left antecubital fossa; soft tricuspid systolic murmur that varies with respiration; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.4 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 210 mg/L (<5); troponin within normal limits; chest X-ray: bilateral peripheral rounded infiltrates; ECG sinus tachycardia; blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours plus vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose
options.rationale: Right-sided IE in an IV drug user is usually Staphylococcus aureus; empirical therapy targets MSSA and MRSA together (flucloxacillin plus vancomycin) until sensitivities are known. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 2.4 g every 4 hours plus gentamicin 4 to 5 mg/kg daily
options.rationale: This is the empirical regimen for native-valve left-sided community-onset endocarditis without staphylococcal risk factors; it undertreats staphylococcal disease in an IV drug user. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus rifampicin as outpatient management now
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inappropriate for endocarditis; parenteral therapy is required until bactericidal control is documented. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours plus gentamicin daily
options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam does not adequately cover MRSA and is not the standard empirical regimen for IE; staphylococcal cover is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily as monotherapy pending culture and echocardiography
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy does not cover staphylococci adequately and misses MRSA in an IV drug user population. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

explanation.summary: Right-sided infective endocarditis in an IV drug user is characteristically caused by Staphylococcus aureus and typically involves the tricuspid valve with septic pulmonary emboli on chest imaging. Australian empirical therapy targets both MSSA and MRSA pending culture results: flucloxacillin plus vancomycin (loading dose then weight-based maintenance). Once organism and sensitivities are known, therapy is narrowed: flucloxacillin monotherapy for MSSA, vancomycin monotherapy for MRSA. Duration is at least 4 weeks IV for uncomplicated right-sided IE, longer for complications. Echocardiography (transthoracic first, transoesophageal if inconclusive or valve surgery being considered) is essential.
key_points: Right-sided IE in IVDU is usually Staph aureus.
Empirical cover: flucloxacillin plus vancomycin for MSSA and MRSA.
Narrow to flucloxacillin (MSSA) or vancomycin (MRSA) on sensitivities.
Uncomplicated right-sided IE requires 4 weeks IV therapy.
explanation.pearls: In an IV drug user with fevers, pulmonary infiltrates and a tricuspid murmur, start empirical flucloxacillin plus vancomycin after two sets of blood cultures; do not use ceftriaxone monotherapy or oral therapy.

stem:
A 26-year-old man attends a sexual health clinic 12 days after a condomless receptive anal sex encounter with a new partner of unknown HIV status. He has had a febrile illness for 4 days with pharyngitis, myalgias, headache and a fine truncal maculopapular rash. He denies genital ulcers. A rapid fourth-generation antibody-antigen combination assay in-clinic is negative. He has never previously been tested for HIV and has not taken PEP.

He has no significant medical history, is on no regular medications, and is otherwise well. He has already agreed to further testing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fine truncal maculopapular rash; pharyngeal erythema without exudate; bilateral non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Fourth-generation HIV Ab-Ag combined assay negative; syphilis serology, hepatitis B/C serology, gonorrhoea and chlamydia PCR sent; monospot pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

options.text: Repeat the fourth-generation antibody-antigen assay in 8 weeks after exposure
options.rationale: The clinical picture is highly suggestive of acute HIV seroconversion; waiting 8 weeks delays diagnosis while transmission risk is highest. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)

options.text: Order HIV Western blot confirmatory testing on the same sample tomorrow morning
options.rationale: Western blot detects antibody, which lags viral RNA; a negative combined assay implies Western blot would also be negative in the window period. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)

options.text: Order CD4 lymphocyte subset counts to look for a fall consistent with primary infection
options.rationale: CD4 counts are not diagnostic in acute infection; they are used for staging established disease and monitoring therapy. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)

options.text: Test for Epstein-Barr virus IgM antibody as most likely alternative cause of the rash
options.rationale: EBV remains a differential but does not rule out acute HIV; failing to test for HIV RNA in this clinical picture would miss primary infection. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)

options.text: Order HIV RNA (viral load) PCR now for detection during the antibody window period
options.rationale: HIV RNA becomes detectable around 10 days post-exposure, before p24 antigen and antibody; RNA is the diagnostic test during the antibody window in symptomatic seroconversion. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)

explanation.summary: The Australian HIV testing algorithm during suspected acute seroconversion uses HIV RNA (viral load) PCR to detect infection during the antibody window period. Fourth-generation antibody-antigen combined assays detect p24 antigen from around 14 to 21 days post-exposure and antibody from 20 to 45 days. HIV RNA becomes detectable earliest, from around 10 days post-exposure. Symptomatic acute seroconversion presents with a mononucleosis-like illness (fever, pharyngitis, rash, lymphadenopathy, myalgia) and represents the period of highest transmission risk. Positive RNA testing should be followed by confirmatory testing and immediate linkage to specialist care and antiretroviral therapy initiation.
key_points: HIV RNA is detectable from around 10 days post-exposure.
Fourth-generation antibody-antigen from 2 to 3 weeks; antibody from 3 to 6 weeks.
Symptomatic seroconversion is the period of highest transmission risk.
Positive RNA triggers immediate linkage to specialist care.
explanation.pearls: In a mononucleosis-like illness with recent condomless anal sex and negative combined assay, order HIV RNA PCR immediately rather than waiting for antibody seroconversion.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV Medicine (ASHM) Guidelines

stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with 24 hours of a red, swollen and exquisitely tender left lower leg after a minor gardening abrasion. Pain is severe and out of proportion to visible skin changes. There are patches of dusky discolouration in the calf and small tense bullae are developing. He has generalised systemic symptoms with rigors.

He last used insulin 8 hours ago. He has no known allergies. Bloods were drawn on arrival and IV access is established.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Left calf red, hot, swollen with dusky patches and small tense bullae; exquisite tenderness; sensation reduced over lateral calf; distal pulses palpable
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.8 x10^9/L (4-11), Hb 118 g/L (135-175), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), glucose 14.2 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110), CRP 342 mg/L (<5), lactate 4.6 mmol/L; LRINEC score 8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Elevate the leg and start oral flucloxacillin 500 mg 6-hourly with community follow-up
options.rationale: The presentation is high probability necrotising soft tissue infection (LRINEC 8); oral outpatient therapy is inappropriate and fatal delay is likely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

options.text: Immediate surgical review for urgent debridement plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
options.rationale: LRINEC score 6 or above is high probability necrotising fasciitis; urgent surgical debridement is the definitive treatment along with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

options.text: MRI leg with contrast to confirm fascial involvement before considering surgical review
options.rationale: Imaging must not delay surgery when clinical suspicion is high; MRI has a role only if surgical decision is genuinely uncertain and delay is not harmful. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

options.text: IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose alone with ward observation and hourly review
options.rationale: Vancomycin monotherapy misses gram-negative and anaerobic cover; NSTI requires triple-agent empirical therapy plus surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

options.text: Skin punch biopsy at the affected calf site for Gram stain and culture before treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy has no acute diagnostic role; deep tissue samples are taken intraoperatively. Delay to biopsy would be fatal in NSTI. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency and diagnosis is primarily clinical. Features raising suspicion include severe pain out of proportion, dusky skin changes, bullae, crepitus, cutaneous anaesthesia, systemic toxicity and rapid progression. The LRINEC score uses CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose to stratify risk; score 6 or above is high probability of NSTI. Definitive treatment is early aggressive surgical debridement combined with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem, plus vancomycin, plus clindamycin for toxin suppression). Imaging must not delay surgery.
key_points: Diagnosis of NSTI is clinical; LRINEC assists risk stratification.
LRINEC 6 or above is high probability.
Surgical debridement is definitive treatment.
Empirical antibiotics: piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin.
explanation.pearls: In a diabetic with pain out of proportion, dusky calf skin, bullae and LRINEC 6 or above, call the surgeon before you order the CT scan; delayed debridement is the leading cause of mortality.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

stem:
A 42-year-old woman with known Addison's disease is brought to ED by her partner with 24 hours of vomiting, abdominal pain and increasing lethargy after a gastroenteritis illness. She takes hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking, 5 mg at midday and 5 mg at 4pm, plus fludrocortisone 100 microgram daily. She has been unable to keep down her morning hydrocortisone dose today. She is drowsy but rousable, feels dizzy on sitting, and looks pigmented.

Her partner reports that she did not double her hydrocortisone dose despite the illness. There is no fever and no localising infective source.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min supine, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg supine, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but oriented; hyperpigmented palmar creases; dry mucous membranes; abdomen soft with mild diffuse tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), creatinine 132 micromol/L (60-110); venous gas pH 7.28, HCO3 14 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg with intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride at 250 mL/hour
options.rationale: Oral steroids are inappropriate when the patient is vomiting; parenteral hydrocortisone is required and prednisolone lacks the mineralocorticoid activity of hydrocortisone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal crisis)

options.text: Increase fludrocortisone to 200 microgram orally and give oral rehydration solution
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not the acute treatment; glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone) is urgent and the patient is vomiting so oral therapy is inappropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal crisis)

options.text: IV dexamethasone 4 mg with intravenous fluid resuscitation and glucose supplementation
options.rationale: Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and hydrocortisone is preferred; dexamethasone is used only if the diagnosis is uncertain and short synacthen test is planned. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal crisis)

options.text: IV noradrenaline infusion to restore blood pressure before hydrocortisone administration
options.rationale: Vasopressors are refractory to steroid deficiency; hydrocortisone must be given first and vasopressors are used only if BP remains inadequate after fluids and steroids. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal crisis)

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg then 200 mg over 24 hours with intravenous fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours (or 50 mg every 6 hours) alongside IV fluid resuscitation and glucose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal crisis)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening emergency in known Addison's disease, often triggered by intercurrent illness or failure of sick-day dose adjustment. Immediate treatment is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours (either continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours), together with 1 litre of 0.9 percent sodium chloride over the first hour and glucose replacement for hypoglycaemia. Hydrocortisone provides both glucocorticoid and adequate mineralocorticoid activity at these doses so separate fludrocortisone is not needed until doses drop below 50 mg per day. Patients should be educated on sick-day rules (double oral dose for febrile illness, IM hydrocortisone if vomiting).
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours.
Hydrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid activity at these doses.
IV fluids: 1 litre 0.9 percent sodium chloride in the first hour.
Sick-day rules: double oral dose or IM hydrocortisone if vomiting.
explanation.pearls: In known Addison's disease with vomiting and hypotension, give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately and 1 litre normal saline in the first hour before any workup; dexamethasone is reserved for undiagnosed cases going for synacthen testing.
